papers.title: NextEval: An Agent-Based Solver and Benchmark for Derivative-Free Optimization
papers.abstract: Derivative-free optimization (DFO) addresses problems where derivatives are unavailable or costly to obtain. This setting often arises in simulation-based and experimental applications, where evaluating the black-box objective can itself be costly. Thus, it remains a central challenge in DFO to effectively exploit accumulated observations to select informative evaluation points under a limited budget. In this light, we introduce the NextEval solver, an agent-based DFO solver, which integrates the capabilities of a large language model (LLM) to guide the sequential selection of evaluation points. Specifically, we establish a system that combines an LLM agent with a numerical environment. The environment provides tools for analyzing past evaluations and executing numerical methods, while maintaining a shared evaluation history and method-specific state to support continuation across method switches. Using observations and tool feedback, the LLM agent selects tools, configures their parameters, and allocates the evaluation budget, while numerical methods compute and evaluate candidate points. Building on this system, we also introduce NextEval Bench, a benchmark protocol for comparing agent configurations on shared DFO tasks using the same numerical tools under matched evaluation budgets and information constraints. Numerical results on low-dimensional DFO problems demonstrate that the NextEval solver outperforms the state-of-the-art DFO baselines in function-evaluation efficiency.

papers.title: QESChunker: A Single Objective Unifies Overlapping and Non-Overlapping Chunking for RAG
papers.abstract: Chunking is a fundamental preprocessing step in retrieval-augmented generation (RAG), yet most existing chunkers rely primarily on heuristics. We introduce the Question--Evidence-Supervised Chunker (QESChunker), to our knowledge the first method for constructing static chunk indices from question--evidence supervision. QESChunker constructs document-specific chunk indices by optimizing over human-annotated or LLM-generated question--evidence pairs, without access to held-out test queries. We formulate non-overlapping and overlapping index construction through a unified question--evidence utility-maximization objective, turning chunking into a supervised combinatorial optimization problem. Under the non-overlap constraint, the objective decomposes over chunks and can be optimized exactly in polynomial time by dynamic programming. When overlap is allowed, the objective becomes monotone submodular; exact optimization is NP-hard, but our greedy achieves a $(1-1/\sqrt{e})$-approximation. Across two self-constructed and three public datasets, both variants outperform existing chunking methods in complete-evidence recall in nearly all evaluated settings, under the same overlap regime and a fixed hybrid retriever. These results recast chunking as supervised, budget-aware index construction for evidence retrieval.

papers.title: MuonGS: Pretraining LLMs with Relaxed Weight-Norm Control
papers.abstract: Weight decay and explicit weight-norm constraints improve optimizer performance in language model pretraining, yet a unified understanding of why such control helps and how much is needed remains incomplete. We analyze norm control in Muon over the entire training trajectory using the \emph{accumulated effective learning rate}, $C_T=\sum_{t<T}\eta_t/\|W_t\|_F$, where $\eta_t$ is the nominal learning rate and $\eta_t/\|W_t\|_F$ is the effective learning rate relative to the weight norm. For bounded update directions, accumulation over any training interval bounds relative weight displacement. We show that vanilla Muon can accumulate only logarithmically, potentially limiting exploration and helping explain its slower empirical progress, whereas MuonW and MuonH guarantee at least linear accumulation under the stated conditions. Going beyond bounded-norm control, we show that sufficiently slow norm growth guarantees faster accumulation than the logarithmic worst case, opening up less restrictive optimizer designs. Based on this insight, we propose MuonGS, which uses Gram--Schmidt (GS) projection to remove the radial component of each Muon update without fixing the weight norm. With bounded update directions and a constant nominal learning rate, we prove that the weight norm grows at most proportionally to $\sqrt{t}$ after $t$ steps. Consequently, MuonGS guarantees $C_T=\Omega(\sqrt{T})$, with accumulation sustained even in later training. Further, for smooth scale-invariant objectives we establish its $O(T^{-1/2})$ stationarity guarantee. In pretraining experiments with 160M- and 400M-parameter dense models as well as a 135M active- and 1B total- parameter MoE model, MuonGS achieves lower validation perplexity than MuonH at long training horizons. In particular, for the dense model it achieves an estimated token-equivalent speedup up to about $15\%$ at matched validation loss to MuonH.

papers.title: The Price of Failure Risk: Clipped Barrier Policy Gradients with Convex Regularization
papers.abstract: Many operations run on a budget that must rarely run out, such as a wear allowance. A wrapper keeps the remaining budget in the state, subtracts a barrier that grows as the budget shrinks and clips the combined reward from below at -m, and a standard policy-gradient learner trains unchanged. The clip level m is a price of failure risk, since the trained value splits exactly into utility before failure, the cost of a margin and the price times the risk, so whatever policy training returns earns the most such utility net of that cost among policies with no greater risk, up to its optimization error. Its risk exceeds a comparison policy's by at most order 1/m when charged costs stay bounded, and value or validation data certify it. The main theoretical result is exponential convergence of the population training flow under any parameter regularizer convex along the motions of the network's units and strong enough against the price, biased toward the prior policy. This extends mean-field convergence of policy gradients from relative entropy to weight decay, which covers continuous-time training of finite networks. Relative entropy adds noise that lets learning leave flat regions, weight decay pulls the parameters toward a reference, and action regularization bounds the risk change by the distance to a trusted rule. Experiments on an exact maintenance benchmark, a fuel-tank controller, a solvable flow and a benchmark-suite task measure the bounds' slack. We state when another method is better, without claiming this one outperforms them.

papers.title: GPU-accelerated wind farm layout search with a distilled endogenous wake model (EndoWake)
papers.abstract: We build on EndoWake, an endogenous wake model that links the wind speed at every grid cell to its upwind neighbors by linear constraints, so that wake field, siting decisions and project constraints share one mixed-integer model. Its four parameters are calibrated once on the single wake of a Reynolds-averaged Navier-Stokes (RANS) simulation, and a graphics processing unit (GPU) scores over a million layouts per second per wind direction. At Lillgrund, we compare searches guided by EndoWake and by PyWake under a RANS judge that no search calls: the fidelity of a wake model is not the quality of the layouts optimized under it. Two diagnostics separate a quadrature error between the sampled wind directions from a surrogate bias localized off each wake edge, not reported before to our knowledge; at random directions, five paired starts detect no difference between the pipelines. The main result puts the speed to use: EndoWake ranks the moves of a local search on the GPU, and PyWake confirms every accepted move. On twenty unseen starts, with one GPU and thirty CPU processes, screen-and-confirm reaches similar mean gains to a search on PyWake alone, 7.9 times faster at one wind speed and 14.9 times faster on the annual energy (3.0 and 4.7 with a proof of local optimality charged to the timed search); on a second site it keeps its speed, and its local optima fall slightly short of those of PyWake alone. Code and data are deposited on Zenodo.

papers.title: A Search-Based Algorithm for Multistage Robust Discrete Linear Optimization and its Implementation
papers.abstract: Robust optimization models that allow decisions to adapt to newly revealed information remain computationally challenging and are often limited to two decision stages or are addressed heuristically or via approximation schemes. This challenge is further amplified when uncertainty sets depend on earlier decisions. Conventional approaches to such problems often require problem-specific reformulations and tailored algorithms, highlighting the need for an exact model-and-run approach. We address this gap by presenting an algorithmic framework for solving multistage robust discrete linear optimization problems. This exact approach adapts and integrates ideas from game-tree search, quantified conflict-driven clause learning, and integer linear programming to explore the minimax tree and is implemented in the open-source solver Yasol. The solver supports discrete decision variables across multiple stages, discrete uncertainty sets with polyhedral or decision-dependent structure, and mixed-integer recourse in the final stage. It can be used as a standalone executable or through a C++ library interface, allowing it to serve as a reference solver for exact methods in multistage robust discrete linear optimization. In an extensive computational study, we demonstrate the capabilities of our solver. The results show competitive performance against a reference approach from the literature for a protection-interdiction problem, as well as strong performance on bilevel benchmark instances. For a multistage cutting-stock problem, we demonstrate the substantial loss in solution quality that can arise from neglecting the multistage structure and show that our solver significantly outperforms decision-rule approximations in terms of computational efficiency while certifying the true multistage optimum.

papers.title: A Graph-informed Kriging model for sample-efficient Bayesian optimization of wind farm layouts
papers.abstract: Wind farm layout optimization becomes increasingly difficult as turbine count grows, especially when high-fidelity aerodynamic models are used. Conventional Kriging-based Bayesian optimization often suffers from low sample efficiency in high-dimensional layout spaces because sparse training data provide limited domain coverage. We develop a Graph-informed Kriging framework that embeds reusable aerodynamic interaction information into the surrogate mean function. The wind farm is represented as a directed aerodynamic graph, where pairwise turbine interactions defined in a low-dimensional relative-coordinate space are assembled into a farm-scale mean. This structured mean captures the dominant variation in annual energy production (AEP), allowing the Gaussian process to model only the residual structure and uncertainty. Numerical experiments show that Graph-informed Kriging consistently improves AEP prediction accuracy over ordinary and generic-trend Kriging under sparse-data conditions, with increasing benefits as layout dimension and wake-interaction strength grow. Embedded in Bayesian optimization, it substantially improves sample efficiency and achieves competitive solutions for the IEA Wind Task 37 benchmark with about 280 AEP evaluations. In a controlled 16-turbine case, it also outperforms ordinary and multi-fidelity Kriging under the same high-fidelity evaluation budget. The framework is further extended to a 48-turbine wind farm, demonstrating applicability to large-scale CFD-based layout optimization. These results show that Graph-informed surrogate modeling can enable more efficient use of high-fidelity aerodynamic models for reliable large-scale wind farm layout design.

papers.title: Minimax-Optimal Small-Loss Bounds for Online Linear Optimisation on $\ell_p$ Balls
papers.abstract: We study full-information online linear optimisation on the unit $\ell_p$ ball in $\mathbb{R}^d$, for fixed $2\le p<\infty$ and losses of dual norm at most one. Let $\Delta_T$ denote the cumulative loss of the best fixed action above each round's minimum. A follow-the-regularised-leader (FTRL) algorithm attains, on every loss sequence and without knowing $T$ or $\Delta_T$, regret $O_p(1+\min\{\Delta_T^{1-1/p},\, d^{1/2-1/p}\sqrt{\Delta_T}\})$. Matching lower bounds show that this rate is minimax for each fixed $p$, and its constant $(2+o(1))p/\log p$ is optimal as $p\to\infty$ among guarantees uniform in $d$ and $T$. The algorithm uses a bounded radial regulariser and switches at most once to its quadratic augmentation. On some paths where follow-the-leader (FTL) has regret one, its regret grows with $T$. A switching extension keeps the sharp constant and also guarantees $\mathrm{Reg}_T\le 2\,\mathrm{Reg}_T^{\mathrm{FTL}}$. For i.i.d. losses whose mean has no zero coordinates, we compute the exact $\log T$ coefficient of the expected regret, which separates FTL's variance term from the bias of the regulariser.

papers.title: AHEAD: Adaptive Neural Acceleration for Large-Scale Linear Programming
papers.abstract: Large-scale linear programs with millions of variables and constraints strain time and memory budgets. First-order methods such as the primal-dual hybrid gradient scale to this regime because they avoid matrix factorizations, but they require many iterations. Learned accelerators can reduce these iterations, yet fewer iterations do not guarantee a shorter solve. Learning inference also takes time, and running the accelerator longer trades solver time for inference time. Existing unrolled accelerators handle this trade-off poorly: each layer processes every variable and constraint, the predicted iterates still need solver refinement, and every instance runs the same layers. We therefore ask: What neural accelerator design achieves end-to-end speedups on large-scale linear programs across sizes and target accuracies? We introduce AHEAD, an accelerator that predicts step sizes for first-order linear programming solvers while keeping their update rules. Its weight-shared predictor reads compact solver statistics and rescales the primal and dual step sizes, so each warm-start iteration stays inexpensive and a short warm-start phase hands the solver a warm start. A learned handoff policy sets the number of warm-start iterations for each instance and target accuracy, after which the solver finishes under its own termination criterion. On packing linear programs with up to $10^7$ variables, AHEAD achieves $6.5$--$11.6\times$ end-to-end speedups over Gurobi's first-order solver from a cold start, including on instances of unseen sizes and distributions. The gains extend to PageRank linear programs and hold across difficulty levels and target accuracies.

papers.title: GNBG-C: A Unified and Configurable Benchmark Generator for Constrained Continuous Optimization
papers.abstract: Many real-world optimization tasks are governed not only by what should be optimized, but also by what is allowed: a solution must first satisfy physical, operational, safety, budgetary, or structural requirements before its objective value becomes meaningful. Yet benchmark design for constrained continuous optimization often treats these restrictions as fixed properties of predefined test instances. Existing generators and benchmark suites provide essential foundations for reproducible comparison, but they either focus primarily on configurable objective landscapes or expose constraint properties within limited, predefined regimes, making it difficult to ask targeted questions about constraint-induced difficulty: whether an optimizer struggles because feasible regions are small, boundaries are restrictive, variables are tightly coupled, or constraint information is poorly scaled. We introduce GNBG-C, a Generalized Numerical Benchmark Generator for Constrained Continuous Optimization. The central idea is to treat the feasible region itself as a configurable object rather than as an inseparable attachment to a fixed test function. By generating controlled constraint regimes around the known GNBG global minimizer, the generator enables systematic studies in which feasibility pressure can be varied while preserving that point as a global minimizer of the constrained problem. This allows researchers to examine how optimizers discover feasibility, handle constraint pressure, and improve objective quality under diverse and controllable feasibility conditions. GNBG-C therefore provides a flexible and auditable framework for probing the strengths and weaknesses of constrained continuous optimizers under targeted forms of feasibility-side difficulty.

papers.title: Balanced Active Subspaces for Optimal Control via Trajectory Optimization
papers.abstract: The curse of dimensionality associated with solving the Hamilton-Jacobi-Bellman equation for the value function remains a key obstacle for real-time optimal feedback control of high-dimensional nonlinear dynamical systems. This is especially severe in aerospace applications such as relaminarizing unsteady turbulent flows and recovering from aerodynamic stall where nonlinear dynamics play a significant role. We introduce Balanced Active Subspaces for Optimal Control (BASOC), a model reduction framework which seeks to find directions in state space along which the value function is most sensitive, and the distribution of states exhibits maximum variance along optimal trajectories. BASOC leverages trajectory optimization and the Pontryagin minimum principle to obtain state and co-state (value function gradient) data along locally optimal trajectories for constructing state and gradient covariance matrices. Balancing these matrices provides an oblique projection for approximating the value function, which can also be used to construct reduced-order models and surrogate feedback control laws. We show that for linear-quadratic optimal control problems, BASOC becomes equivalent to a snapshot method for initial condition balancing of the optimally controlled closed-loop realization. The framework is demonstrated on a nonlinear three-dimensional system where POD and balanced truncation are known to perform poorly, and on the nonlinear complex Ginzburg-Landau equation to demonstrate feasibility for larger-scale systems.

papers.title: Frequency-Uniform Log-Regret Reinforcement Learning for Diffusions
papers.abstract: High-frequency control problems are often studied through time discretization, but refining the timestep $\delta$ increases the discrete horizon $H=T/\delta$ and can make standard finite-horizon regret guarantees deteriorate even when the physical horizon $T$ is fixed. We study episodic value-based reinforcement learning for Euler discretizations of controlled diffusions. The performance is measured as the cumulative regret over $K$ episodes relative to the optimal policy of the corresponding Euler model. Under stability and regularity conditions on value function gradients, Bellman residual derivatives, and fitted critics, we prove an $\mathcal{O}(\log K)$ regret bound with constants uniform in $\delta$. For dynamics with drift linear in unknown parameters and unknown constant diffusion covariance, we verify localized versions of these conditions for a constrained, model-based controlled-diffusion fitted-$Q$ algorithm (CD-FQ) and obtain high-probability $\mathcal{O}(\log K\log\log K)$ regret for fixed and finite $T$, again with constants uniform in $\delta$.

papers.title: NAG-GS: A Semi-Implicit Stochastic Optimizer with Large-Step Stability
papers.abstract: Stochastic first-order methods are widely used for large-scale optimization and machine learning, where their performance often depends on the learning rate. We study NAG-GS, a stochastic momentum method based on a semi-implicit Gauss--Seidel discretization of a Nesterov-type flow. For strongly convex quadratics, we determine the exact range of stable step sizes for fixed damping and the step size that minimizes the worst-case spectral radius. When the damping equals the strong-convexity parameter, the method recovers the accelerated asymptotic factor $(\sqrt{\kappa}-1)/(\sqrt{\kappa}+1)$, where $\kappa$ is the condition number. We also prove that the quadratic iteration converges linearly with dynamic damping when its limiting fixed-damping iteration is stable. For general strongly convex, possibly nonsmooth objectives, we establish an $O(1/k)$ bound on the expected objective gap of the last iterate, using a conditionally unbiased stochastic first-order oracle with bounded second moment. The result holds with dynamic damping from any $\gamma_0>0$. We show that NAG-GS can also be written as a Heavy-Ball iteration with explicitly determined step sizes and momentum coefficients. We test the stochastic result on nonsmooth hinge-loss classification problems, and further evaluate NAG-GS on quadratic problems, logistic regression, convolutional neural networks, RoBERTa, and Vision Transformers. The experiments show that NAG-GS can remain effective at learning rates where standard optimizers become unstable or lose accuracy.

papers.title: A derivative-free trust-region approach for Low Order-Value Optimization problems
papers.abstract: The Low Order-Value Optimization (LOVO) problem involves minimizing the minimum among a finite number of function values within a feasible set. LOVO has several practical applications such as robust parameter estimation, protein alignment, portfolio optimization, among others. In this work, we are interested in the constrained nonlinear optimization LOVO problem of minimizing the minimum between a finite number of function values subject to a nonempty closed convex set where each function is a black-box and continuously differentiable, but the derivatives are not available. We develop the first derivative-free trust-region algorithm for constrained LOVO problems with convergence to weakly critical points. Under suitable conditions, we establish the global convergence of the algorithm and also its worst-case iteration complexity analysis. An initial open-source implementation using only linear interpolation models is developed. Extensive numerical experiments and comparison with existing alternatives show the properties and the efficiency of the proposed approach when solving LOVO problems.

papers.title: Learning Sequential Decisions from Multiple Sources via Group-Robust Markov Decision Processes
papers.abstract: Learning a common policy from multiple source environments requires accounting for cross-source heterogeneity, and the offline setting introduces an additional challenge of limited data coverage. We formulate this problem as a distributionally robust Markov decision process under a shared linear MDP representation with source-specific transition and reward components. The uncertainty set is constructed through feature-wise mixtures of these components, yielding a $d$-rectangular structure that captures cross-source heterogeneity and admits a robust Bellman recursion. Building on this formulation, we develop Group-Robust Pessimistic Value Iteration (GR-PEVI), an offline policy-learning algorithm that combines feature-wise worst-case aggregation with a data-dependent pessimism penalty. Under a robust partial coverage condition, we establish finite-sample suboptimality guarantees for GR-PEVI and extend the analysis to clustered sources, characterizing the trade-off between the statistical gain from pooling similar sources and the approximation error induced by within-cluster heterogeneity. Simulation studies demonstrate the effectiveness of GR-PEVI, with empirical behavior consistent with the theoretical analysis. We apply GR-PEVI to a multi-source electronic health record study of multiple sclerosis treatment decisions to illustrate its use in a clinical setting.

papers.title: Learning to Control: The iUzawa-Net for Nonsmooth Optimal Control of Linear PDEs
papers.abstract: We propose an optimization-informed deep neural network approach, named iUzawa-Net, aiming for the first solver that enables real-time solutions for a class of nonsmooth optimal control problems of linear partial differential equations (PDEs). The iUzawa-Net unrolls an inexact Uzawa method for saddle point problems, replacing classical preconditioners and PDE solvers with specifically designed learnable neural networks. We prove universal approximation properties and establish the asymptotic $\varepsilon$-optimality for the iUzawa-Net, and validate its promising numerical efficiency through nonsmooth elliptic and parabolic optimal control problems. Our techniques offer a versatile framework for designing and analyzing various optimization-informed deep learning approaches to optimal control and other PDE-constrained optimization problems. The proposed learning-to-control approach synergizes model-based optimization algorithms and data-driven deep learning techniques, inheriting the merits of both methodologies.

papers.title: Phases of Muon: When Muon Eclipses SignSGD
papers.abstract: Muon and related spectral optimizers have recently demonstrated strong empirical performance as scalable stochastic methods, often outperforming Adam. Yet their behavior remains poorly understood. We analyze stochastic Muon, which orthogonalizes an exponential moving average of minibatch gradients, on a high-dimensional matrix-valued least squares problem, and we compare it with stochastic SignSGD, a simple baseline comparable to Adam. We derive explicit deterministic dynamics that provide a tractable framework for studying learning behavior. We show that Muon has non-linear sensitivity to the effective batch $B_{\rm eff}=B(1+\beta)/(1-\beta)$. With exact whitening and small $B_{\rm eff}$ Muon fails to resolve smaller eigenmodes, slowing down convergence. Momentum and finite Newton--Shulz iterations can act as a ridge which lessen this effect. This behavior is in contrast with SignSGD which has no transition, leading to different optimal learning rates, but with matching convergence rate up to a constant factor in the isotropic setting. For anisotropic data, large batch setting Muon performs a square-root preconditioning with respect to the data covariance spectrum while SignSGD provides no preconditioning for generic covariances. We analyze time to target loss in a power law covariance model and derive a phase diagram in the data exponent $\alpha$ and target exponent $\zeta$. Muon is favored for steep covariance spectra with rich targets ($\alpha>2$, $\zeta<\alpha+1$), SignSGD is favored for flat spectra ($\alpha<1$), and in other regions the winner depends on how the target loss scales with dimension. Our results shed light on why replacing Adam with Muon is not trivial even from a pure optimization perspective.

papers.title: Computational and Statistical Guarantees of the c-Rectified flow
papers.abstract: Recently, rectified flow has emerged as a fundamental framework for large-scale image generation, powering state-of-the-art systems such as FLUX.1 and Stable Diffusion 3. Despite its remarkable empirical success, the computational and statistical guarantees of iterative rectified flow have remained largely unexplored. We address this problem by studying c-rectified flow, a cost-aware class of rectified flow that projects velocity fields onto a gradient class while preserving endpoint marginals. The ordinary rectified flow can fail to recover the optimal transport coupling: in a Gaussian case study, the iteration converges to the optimal coupling if and only if the source and target covariance matrices commute. More generally, for a Gaussian to log-concave coupling, the ordinary rectified flow can reach a fixed point after one step from independent initialization. In contrast, under suitable regularity and uniform-integrability assumptions, iterative c-rectified flow always converges to the optimal transport coupling. We further establish quantitative one-step contraction and exponential convergence guarantees under projection-stability assumptions for both quadratic and strongly convex displacement costs. Finally, under a H\"older ball assumption, we develop new minimax-optimal score estimation rates and show that, when combined with iterative c-rectified flow, they yield a rate-optimal estimator of the optimal transport for the dimension \(d \ge 3\) and a nearly parametric rate for \(d=1,2\).

papers.title: Momentum in large-batch training: Polyak enlarges the critical batch size, Nesterov improves data efficiency
papers.abstract: We study when and how momentum improves large-batch training in the one-pass regime, using power-law kernel regression as a tractable setting. We first characterize stochastic stability through the \emph{critical learning rate}, defined as the largest learning rate for stable training, and obtain $\eta_{\mathrm{SGD}}^{\mathrm{crit}}\eqsim 1$, $\eta_{\mathrm{Polyak}}^{\mathrm{crit}}\eqsim \min\{1,B(1-\beta)\}$, and $\eta_{\mathrm{Nesterov}}^{\mathrm{crit}}\eqsim \min\{1,B^q(1-\beta)\}$, where $B$ is the batch size, $\beta\in[0,1)$ is the momentum factor, and \(q>1\) is the capacity exponent governing spectral decay. Within the stable region, we derive scaling laws for the full risk dynamics, capturing the progression from an early transient through power-law decay to a noise floor. We then optimize the final-step risk under a fixed data budget, obtaining a three-regime phase diagram that reveals how the benefits of momentum change with batch size. Notably, Polyak enlarges the critical batch size, the largest batch size preserving the optimal small-batch data-scaling exponent, thereby allowing fewer sequential updates without sacrificing data efficiency. In contrast, Nesterov improves the optimal data-scaling exponent in the large-batch regime through look-ahead-induced suppression of noise amplification. Experiments on PLK regression quantitatively support the theoretical scaling predictions, while neural-network experiments provide qualitative evidence for the predicted batch-size dependence and stability behavior.

papers.title: SD-DPC: Sparse Dictionary Differentiable Predictive Control
papers.abstract: We present sparse dictionary differentiable predictive control (SD-DPC), a framework for learning sparse, interpretable feedback policies for nonlinear systems from data. A prediction model is first identified by rollout-based sparse identification of nonlinear dynamics (SINDy), building on gradient-based and multistep formulations. The policy is then parameterized as a sparse combination of dictionary functions and trained by differentiating a constrained finite-horizon predictive-control objective through this model, so that its terms are selected by closed-loop performance rather than by imitating a previously trained controller. The result is an explicit feedback law with only a handful of terms. Across three benchmark control problems, SD-DPC satisfies the constraints in almost all test scenarios, outperforms a policy distilled onto the same terms by up to an order of magnitude, and requires orders of magnitude less memory and online computation than an optimization benchmark, while admitting explicit sensitivity bounds.

papers.title: Multi-time-scale Control of Power Systems
papers.abstract: The power grid has been dominated by large synchronous generators and clearly separated control layers. Today, power-electronics energy conversion interfaces are rapidly being deployed calling for another look at system-level control hierarchies. This article examines how multi-time-scale modeling, feedback control, and feedback optimization can help reinterpret the traditional organically grown hierarchy of primary control, automatic generation control, and economic dispatch, and enable new approaches for control of contemporary power systems. Beginning with an overview of power system models and conventional operational practices, the article develops connections to modern control architectures that can coordinate heterogeneous resources, account for operational constraints, and exploit faster actuation without overlooking first-principles physics.

papers.title: Verifying Control Invariance of H-Polytopes is coNP-Complete
papers.abstract: We prove that verifying whether an H-polytope is control invariant for a discrete-time linear system with polytopic input constraints is \textsc{coNP}-complete. This establishes a fundamental computational complexity barrier for set-theoretic control. As an immediate consequence, the exact computation of maximal control invariant subsets of H-polytopes is \textsc{coNP}-hard. These hardness results hold regardless of whether the input constraint set is given in H- or V-representation.

papers.title: A model predictive control framework with robust stability guarantees under unbounded disturbances
papers.abstract: To address feasibility issues in model predictive control (MPC), most implementations relax state constraints by using slack variables and adding a penalty to the cost. We propose an alternative strategy: relaxing the initial state constraint with a penalty. Compared to state-of-the-art soft constrained MPC formulations, the proposed formulation has two key features: (i) input-to-state stability and bounds on the cumulative constraint violation for unbounded disturbances; (ii) close-to-optimal performance under nominal operating conditions. The idea is initially presented for open-loop asymptotically stable nonlinear systems by designing the penalty as a Lyapunov function, but we also show how to relax this condition to: i) Lyapunov stable systems; ii) stabilizable systems; and iii) utilizing an implicit characterization of the Lyapunov function. In the special case of linear systems, the proposed MPC formulation reduces to a quadratic program, and the offline design and online computational complexity are only marginally increased compared to a nominal design. Numerical examples demonstrate benefits compared to state-of-the-art soft-constrained MPC formulations.

papers.title: Perturbed Gradient Descent Algorithms are Small-Disturbance Input-to-State Stable
papers.abstract: This article investigates the robustness of gradient descent algorithms under perturbations. The concept of small-disturbance input-to-state stability (ISS) for discrete-time nonlinear dynamical systems is introduced, along with its Lyapunov characterization. The conventional linear Polyak-Lojasiewicz (PL) condition is then extended to a nonlinear version, and it is shown that the gradient descent algorithm is small-disturbance ISS provided the objective function satisfies the generalized nonlinear PL condition. This small-disturbance ISS property guarantees that the gradient descent algorithm converges to a small neighborhood of the optimum under sufficiently small perturbations. As a direct application of the developed framework, we demonstrate that the LQR cost satisfies the generalized nonlinear PL condition, thereby establishing that the policy gradient algorithm for LQR is small-disturbance ISS. Additionally, other popular policy gradient algorithms, including natural policy gradient and Gauss-Newton method, are also proven to be small-disturbance ISS.

papers.title: Optimization of the second Robin eigenvalue on a planar exterior domain under fixed area constraint
papers.abstract: We consider the Robin Laplacian on a planar exterior domain with a negative boundary parameter. For a negative boundary parameter of a sufficiently large absolute value this operator has at least two negative eigenvalues below the bottom of the essential spectrum. We prove that under a fixed area constraint and convexity assumption on the bounded complement of the exterior domain the second Robin eigenvalue is maximized by the exterior of the disk. The inequality is strict for every exterior of a non-circular domain whenever the comparison disk has a negative second eigenvalue. The proof modifies the parallel-coordinate method by allowing the angular phase of a trial function to vary with the distance from the boundary. This result resolves the first item in a 2024 conjecture by the authors under an additional convexity assumption. Relaxing the convexity and the perimeter constraint remain open problems.

papers.title: Observability of wave equations with time- and space-dependent potentials: a counterexample under GCC and a positive criterion on the disk
papers.abstract: We show that the geometric control condition (GCC) does not guarantee internal observability for a wave equation with a smooth time-dependent potential. On a bounded connected domain with analytic boundary, we construct a nonempty open observation set such that the pair satisfies GCC and the free Dirichlet wave is observable. For this same domain and observation set, we construct a smooth $2\pi$-periodic potential for which there exists a nonzero smooth Dirichlet wave that vanishes on the observed cylinder for all time. The wave is the unique mild solution in the space $X_\Omega=L^2(\Omega)\times H^{-1}(\Omega)$ on every finite time interval, so no finite observation horizon yields an observability inequality for this fixed potential. The construction starts from a real-valued local counterexample to unique continuation across a noncharacteristic hyperplane. This local statement is of independent interest, since earlier constructions for the wave operator use complex-valued waves and potentials. The global counterexample is then obtained by joining flat oscillatory solutions along the edges of a polygonal observation set, repairing their sum at the vertices without changing its zero set, and using a spatial transition to a common time-independent pair near the boundary. The planar construction also yields counterexamples in every space dimension $n\ge3$. For comparison, and to identify a geometry that supplies both propagation and continuation, we show on the unit disk that an observation region containing a central disk and a neighborhood of an embedded cross-cut yields observability for every weak wave at sufficiently large observation time, with constants uniform over bounded measurable potentials. The proof uses a cut, logarithmic polar coordinates, and a Carleman weight whose favorable flux is confined to the observed artificial boundary.

papers.title: Demand Estimation with Unobserved Stockout Substitution: Exact Likelihood Maximization
papers.abstract: When a product is sold out, customers who prefer it may buy a substitute or leave without purchasing. Efficient demand estimation in this setting is challenging when inventory is observed only at replenishments, because the stockout times, and hence the products available to each customer, are unobserved. Estimating demand efficiently under stockout substitution has been a challenging problem since Anupindi et al. (1998), and it has become more pressing as the scale of such problem instances grows thanks to innovations in retailing such as unmanned stores. We provide a complete solution to this problem for the multinomial logit (MNL) model, the most widely used model of customer choice. Using a continuous-time representation of the purchase process developed in Zhou et al. (2026), we show that the exact likelihood and its gradient are one-dimensional integrals, no matter how many products, customers, or stockouts there are. Both can be evaluated at a cost linear in the numbers of products and periods. Our method estimates demand for 2,000 products from 2,000 selling periods in under ten minutes.

papers.title: Linear Programming Upper Bounds for the Coil-in-the-Box Problem
papers.abstract: Let $S_n$ denote the maximum length of a coil in the $n$-dimensional hypercube $Q_n$, i.e., a simple cycle whose induced subgraph has no additional chords. We combine classical square-counting identities and structural properties of maximum coils with new valid combinatorial inequalities into a parameterized linear program whose optimal value provides an upper bound for $S_n$. For $n\ge13$, we construct two analytic dual feasible solutions. Their objective values yield upper bounds on $S_n$, and the smaller value is the exact optimum of the parameterized LP. One dual solution results in the bound \[ S_n\le 2^{n-1} \frac{8n(n-1)(5n-14)} {40n^3-131n^2+4n+136-(5n-14)\lfloor3n/4\rfloor}, \] which improves upon the upper bounds in Lukito, Lukito-van Zanten, and Z\'emor for $13\le n\le19853$. The second yields the upper bound \[ S_n\le 2^{n-1}\left( 1-\frac1{30\sqrt{3n}}+O(n^{-1}) \right), \] improving upon the asymptotic upper bound of Z\'emor. Taken together, the two bounds improve upon the upper bounds for $S_n$ in Lukito, Lukito-van Zanten, and Z\'emor for every $n\ge13$.

papers.title: From Global Optimization to Exact Coordinates: Heilbronn's Triangle Problem on the Unit Square Using Mixed-Integer Nonlinear Optimization
papers.abstract: We develop a mixed-integer nonlinear programming (MINLP) approach for the Heilbronn triangle problem on the unit square. The formulation exploits the boundary structure of optimal configurations, which we establish rigorously, to fix coordinates and orientation variables a priori. With this formulation, a general-purpose global solver solves the case $n=9$ to global optimality within its numerical tolerances in about eight minutes on a laptop and without any precomputation, compared with about 23 hours of total computation for the best previous approach. The same model also solves $n=10$ for the first time, in under seven hours, and confirms the configuration of Comellas and Yebra (2002). The numerical solutions then guide an exact symbolic reconstruction, and the minimum triangle area of every reconstructed configuration is verified in exact arithmetic. This yields exact coordinates for all $n\le 10$, including the configurations of Comellas and Yebra (2002) for $n=9$ and $n=10$, together with rigorous lower bounds. Finally, we derive structural properties of optimal configurations, formulate a conjecture on the number of critical triangles, and pose an open question. All code and data are publicly available.

papers.title: Theoretical and Computational Advances in Birkhoff Pseudospectral Transcription for Aerospace Optimal Control
papers.abstract: Birkhoff pseudospectral methods replace the differentiation matrices of classical transcriptions with integration operators whose conditioning does not deteriorate with polynomial order. This paper presents theoretical and computational advancements toward their practical use in aerospace optimal control. The initial-point-anchored Birkhoff integration operator is constructed explicitly for flipped Legendre-Gauss-Radau grids and related exactly to the corresponding Lagrange differentiation matrix and, through a reflection, to the standard Radau Birkhoff operator, whose conditioning properties it inherits. Rate constraints on nonlinear functions of states and controls are enforced directly through the pseudospectral operators and, for control-rate limits, shown to be primal and dual equivalent to state augmentation. Non-affine time mappings concentrate the nodes around localized trajectory features, and composing affine scaling and equilibration transformations provides a systematic way to construct scaling strategies. The methods are implemented in the open-source MATLAB framework RAPTOR and tested across a range of challenging optimal control problems, including a dense-grid orbit-raising problem, a rate-limited landing scenario, a Space Shuttle entry problem, and a five-phase reusable-launch-vehicle mission.
